overview: This file traces U.S. and Allied occupation policy toward Japanese telecommunications and radar from the immediate postwar period through 1949. Its early documents concern restoring official telegraph links between Japan and Allied, neutral, and co-belligerent governments; later papers progressively reopen international, commercial, and ship-to-shore communications while retaining censorship, payment, and foreign-exchange controls. A substantial 1949 group records the conflict between restrictions on Japanese possession of radar as military equipment and the commercial need to install imported navigational radar aboard export ships. The bundle concludes with a 1946 covering letter and duplicate copies of a 1945 technical-intelligence report on wartime radar research at the Sumitomo Research Laboratory. Although the file title gives an ending date of January 16, 1946, the assembled papers extend through December 1949.

subfiles.title: Turner memorandum on telegraphic communications with Japan
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Francis Colt de Wolf, Telecommunications Division
subfiles.about: Requests advice on arranging commercial transmission of foreign-government messages to representatives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Turner forwards the State Department's December 26 memorandum, the War Department's January 9 reply, and CINCAFPAC's January 8 telegram. He explains that French and Swiss complaints prompted the inquiry and criticizes the CINCAFPAC response as having misunderstood the problem. He asks how commercial companies can be authorized to accept prepaid or collect official messages.

subfiles.title: State Department request for foreign-government telegraph service to Japan
subfiles.from: Acting Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs, State Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, Operations Division, War Department
subfiles.about: Requests authorization for Allied, neutral, and co-belligerent governments to communicate commercially with their representatives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department reports uncertainty among commercial telegraph companies because no general authorization covers non-U.S. government traffic to and from Japan. It cites Swiss insistence on coded communication, British use of a guard ship in Tokyo Bay, and other governments' reliance on U.S. agencies. The Department recommends unrestricted official traffic in code or plain language between foreign governments and their representatives in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: War Department reply on commercial telegraph service
subfiles.from: R. L. Vittrup, for the Secretary of War
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Acting Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Responds that existing circuits are adequate and raises the need for Treasury-approved financial-settlement procedures.
subfiles.summary: The War Department forwards General MacArthur's assessment that numerous official circuits already serve Japan and that no additional facilities are presently needed. It agrees that the Treasury Department must determine how Japanese and American carriers will settle accounts. The printed year 1945 is evidently an error; the surrounding correspondence establishes the date as January 9, 1946.

subfiles.title: CINCAFPAC telegram on communications circuits with Japan
subfiles.from: CINCAFPAC, Advance Headquarters, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes existing official and press circuits and the conditions for expanding government traffic between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: The telegram lists uncensored official links from Japan to Geneva, Stockholm, Lisbon, Moscow, Bern, and Seoul, as well as British, press, and regional services. Headquarters judges the existing facilities adequate but has no objection to official U.S.-Japan government traffic. It recommends that non-U.S. official messages from Japan be collect and those to Japan prepaid, pending Treasury arrangements between carriers.

subfiles.title: Routing note for British Embassy submission
subfiles.from: M. D. S.
subfiles.about: Records delivery of a British Embassy paper following an earlier telephone conversation.
subfiles.summary: The brief annotation states that a British Embassy representative brought the accompanying material for Mr. Emerson. J. T. C. had advised the representative to put the matter in writing after a telephone conversation the previous week.

subfiles.title: British aide-mémoire on Japanese coastal wireless facilities
subfiles.from: British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.about: Requests Washington's authorization for British ships to use re-established Japanese ship-to-shore wireless facilities.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy reports that SCAP's Civil Communications Section is restoring Japanese coastal wireless service for Allied shipping. Because British traffic in Japanese waters is growing, the British government welcomes the facilities but understands that Washington must authorize their official use. It asks that British shipping receive the necessary authority.

subfiles.title: Draft message to SCAP on British use of coastal wireless
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests transmission of a draft message supporting British access to Japanese coastal wireless facilities.
subfiles.summary: The proposed telegram summarizes the British Embassy's request concerning restored coastal stations. The State and War Departments believe SCAP already possesses authority to approve their use without further reference to Washington. The draft states that the United States has no objection and asks SCAP to report its action.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1325 transmitting SCAPIN 1771
subfiles.from: Counselor of Mission, Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a SCAP directive revising and relaxing international telecommunications restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses five copies of SCAPIN 1771, dated September 9, 1947. It characterizes the directive as a revision and, in some cases, relaxation of restrictions imposed on Japanese international telecommunications.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1771 relaxing international telecommunications restrictions
subfiles.from: R. M. Levy, for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Rescinds or revises earlier occupation directives governing codes, censorship, commercial messages, and international communications.
subfiles.summary: The directive permits languages, codes, and ciphers accepted by the destination country while retaining SCAP's power to censor domestic and international traffic. It broadens personal, family, business, financial, commercial, and transactional messaging but prohibits transfers of funds, concealment of external assets, and unauthorized dealings in intellectual-property rights. It also revises special services for the United Seamen's Service and American International Underwriters and allows direct administrative contact with the Japanese Ministry of Communications.

subfiles.title: Information memorandum explaining SCAPIN 1771
subfiles.from: A. J. Rehe, Assistant Adjutant General
subfiles.to: SCAP distribution, less the Japanese Government
subfiles.about: Explains the policy rationale and general application of the relaxation of telecommunications controls.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that restrictions are being relaxed to foster foreign trade. It explains that specific prohibited subjects replace the former general definition of transactional messages and that restrictions on languages, codes, and ciphers have largely been removed. Rules governing radiotelegraph messages are also declared applicable to radiotelephone conversations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1379 on ship-shore service for trade representatives
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a directive expanding payment arrangements for Japanese ship-shore telegraphic service.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports that SCAPIN 1603/3 amends an earlier coastal-radio directive. Messages may now be prepaid by any person or organization authorized to use U.S. Military Payment Certificates or Foreign Trade Payment Certificates. The change is intended to facilitate the work of authorized private trade representatives.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1603/3 amending coastal-radio payment rules
subfiles.from: R. M. Levy, for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Authorizes additional prepaid ship-shore messages involving U.S.-registered ships and foreign-trade payment certificates.
subfiles.summary: The directive expands acceptable full-rate messages between persons aboard U.S.-registered ships and persons or organizations in Japan. It adds Foreign Trade Payment Certificates to the previously permitted U.S. Military Payment Certificates. It also authorizes the Japanese Board of Trade to use the same payment provisions for coastal-radio messages to U.S.-registered vessels.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 51 on service for Norwegian merchant shipping
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a SCAP directive extending Japanese ship-shore radio service to Norwegian merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: The despatch follows the earlier report on facilities for foreign-trade representatives. It encloses five copies of SCAPIN 1603/4, dated January 13, 1948, directing the Japanese Government to provide coastal-radio service to Norwegian merchant shipping.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1603/4 extending coastal radio to Norwegian ships
subfiles.from: R. M. Levy, for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Orders the immediate extension of Japanese coastal-radio service to Norwegian merchant shipping.
subfiles.summary: The directive brings Norwegian vessels within the coastal-radio system established for Allied merchant shipping. It states that acceptable traffic, charges, accounting, and settlement procedures are specified in an attached enclosure. Direct communication between SCAP staff and the Japanese Ministry of Communications is authorized.

subfiles.title: Accounting and message rules for Norwegian ship-shore traffic
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Specifies permissible messages, rates, currencies, and accounting procedures for Norwegian ship-shore communications.
subfiles.summary: Permissible traffic includes arrival estimates, vessel control, shipping information, distress and navigation notices, and full-rate personal or organizational messages. Charges are stated in International Communications Gold Francs, while payment in Japan must be made in yen. The Norwegian Telegraph Board and Japanese Ministry of Communications must submit monthly accounts through SCAP, and settlement requires SCAP authorization.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of SCAPIN 1603/4
subfiles.from: R. M. Levy, for the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Duplicates the directive extending Japanese coastal-radio service to Norwegian merchant shipping.
subfiles.summary: This is a second copy of the directive reproduced on page 16. It orders immediate service for Norwegian merchant vessels and refers to an enclosure for permitted traffic, rates, and settlement arrangements.

subfiles.title: Duplicate accounting enclosure for Norwegian ship-shore traffic
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Duplicates the detailed regulations for Norwegian merchant-shipping radio messages and accounts.
subfiles.summary: This second copy repeats the authorized message categories and per-word charges for land-line, coastal-station, and ship-station service. It also repeats the prepayment, yen-conversion, monthly-accounting, and SCAP-approval requirements.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 909 on relaxation of SCAP radar policy
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the modification of SCAP policy to permit navigational radar aboard commercial vessels built in Japan for export.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that SCAP-approved shipbuilding contracts and State Department export licenses for four Maersk Line radars conflicted with JCS restrictions classifying radar as Japanese war potential. The Maersk Line insisted on installation in Japan and threatened a claim if the contracts could not be fulfilled, while Danish diplomatic representatives supported its position. After disagreement among SCAP sections and the naval command, the Commander in Chief approved a distinction between commercial navigational radar and prohibited military radar.

subfiles.title: CCS check note announcing limited radar-policy relaxation
subfiles.from: Civil Communications Section
subfiles.to: MCS, with distribution to CTS, DS, S-2, and S-3
subfiles.about: Explains the Commander in Chief's decision to permit navigational radar while maintaining prohibitions on military applications.
subfiles.summary: The note records approval of a limited relaxation allowing Japanese access to radar as an aid to safe surface navigation. It excludes air-search, fire-control, fighter-direction, altitude-finding, rapid fire-control calculation, airborne, and antiaircraft radar. Contemporary foreign-made marine radar using PPI-type indicators is considered permissible.

subfiles.title: CCS recommendation for the Maersk Line radar installations
subfiles.from: Civil Communications Section
subfiles.about: Recommends a one-time exception permitting installation of four imported radars aboard ships being built for the Danish Maersk Line.
subfiles.summary: CCS recounts that earlier permission for Japanese technicians to install imported navigational radar had been rejected, yet SCAP shipbuilding approvals and State Department export licenses allowed four units to be shipped. One radar had already been impounded and three more were expected, creating possible legal liability and embarrassment. The section recommends supervised installation as a one-time exception and asks the Economic and Scientific Section to report other planned radar or fathometer installations.

subfiles.title: Chief of Staff decision treating commercial radar as a navigational aid
subfiles.from: Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Directs that commercial-vessel radar be treated as a peacetime aid to navigation rather than automatically as prohibited war equipment.
subfiles.summary: The Chief of Staff argues that radar has become common in air and surface navigation since JCS 87 was written. Installation of imported equipment is therefore approved, although Japanese development, manufacture, and assembly remain prohibited. Installations must be supervised by SCAP or by representatives of the supplying company.

subfiles.title: CCS warning on prohibited radar imports
subfiles.from: Civil Communications Section
subfiles.about: Requests notification to the State Department that existing SCAP policy prohibits the importation and Japanese installation of commercial radar.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the State Department licensed four Raytheon navigational radars for export to Japan despite SCAP's restrictive interpretation of JCS 87. One unit had been impounded in Kobe and two more were expected to be seized on arrival. CCS asks the Diplomatic Section to notify Washington before the Eighth Army is instructed to prevent unloading further foreign-made radar.

subfiles.title: Extract from JCS Serial 87 on Japanese industrial war potential
subfiles.from: Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Defines radar as a combat end-product and sets occupation restrictions on Japanese military-industrial capacity.
subfiles.summary: The extract classifies ultra-shortwave radio equipment, specifically radar, as a combat-equipment end-product alongside weapons, warships, armored vehicles, and aircraft. It prohibits Japanese development, manufacture, assembly, or possession of such equipment except when authorized by the Supreme Commander for occupation purposes after consultation with the Allied Council for Japan.

subfiles.title: CCS proposal clarifying the JCS radar directive
subfiles.from: Civil Communications Section
subfiles.about: Proposes a distinction between prohibited radar and permissible radio, industrial, scientific, meteorological, and navigational applications.
subfiles.summary: CCS describes competing interpretations ranging from a ban on every pulsed-radio device to permission for peaceful uses. It recommends allowing communications equipment, industrial radio-frequency apparatus, ionospheric measurements, meteorological pulse devices, and individually approved navigational radar. It also proposes allowing imported radar to be installed by Japanese technicians aboard export ships with case-by-case approval.

subfiles.title: Chief of Staff clarification of permissible radio and radar activity
subfiles.from: Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Approves broad civilian radio and scientific uses while requiring individual approval for Japanese navigational radar.
subfiles.summary: The Chief of Staff rules that JCS Serial 87 refers specifically to radar and does not restrict ordinary communications-radio research, design, manufacture, or use. Industrial radio-frequency processes, ionospheric measurements, meteorological pulse devices, and case-by-case navigational radar are permitted. The decision omits the proposed authorization for Japanese installation of imported radar on foreign-owned export ships, leaving the issue that later produced the Maersk dispute.

subfiles.title: Otterman letter transmitting the Sumitomo radar report
subfiles.from: Harvey B. Otterman, Telecommunications Division
subfiles.to: Cleveland Norcross, Office of Scientific Research and Development
subfiles.about: Sends a report on wartime radar research at the Sumitomo Research Laboratory.
subfiles.summary: Otterman confirms a telephone conversation with Norcross's secretary and encloses the November 3, 1945 investigation report. He notes that it concerns radar-research activities conducted at the Japanese laboratory during the war. The drafting notation establishes March 25, 1946 as the letter date, with a copy sent March 26.

subfiles.title: Investigation report on the Sumitomo Research Laboratory
subfiles.from: Harold C. Wich, Technical Liaison and Investigation Division
subfiles.to: Director, Technical Liaison and Investigation Division
subfiles.about: Reports an investigation of the organization and wartime radar projects of the Sumitomo Research Laboratory at Noborito.
subfiles.summary: Wich describes the laboratory's communications, vacuum-tube, testing, and administrative divisions and its work on the Taki 2, Taki 34, and Tachi 22 radars. Shimizu stated that the Taki 34 used a five-centimeter magnetron and incorporated components copied from a B-29 radar. A July 1945 field model tested at Ajiro near Atami had inadequate range and detail and was reportedly destroyed when the war ended; attempted jamming tests were unsuccessful.

subfiles.title: Duplicate investigation report on the Sumitomo Research Laboratory
subfiles.from: Harold C. Wich, Technical Liaison and Investigation Division
subfiles.to: Director, Technical Liaison and Investigation Division
subfiles.about: Duplicates the technical-intelligence report concerning wartime radar work at the Sumitomo laboratory.
subfiles.summary: This compared copy repeats the laboratory organization and the allocation of projects by the Tama Laboratory. It again records development of the Taki 2 and Taki 34, extensive work on the Tachi 22, copying of B-29 radar components, the Ajiro field test, and the reported destruction of the experimental equipment after Japan's surrender.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how occupation communications policy evolved from strict military control into a regulated infrastructure for diplomacy, trade, personal traffic, and merchant shipping. The 1949 radar papers expose a revealing clash between demilitarization rules, interagency disagreement, commercial contracts, diplomatic pressure, and the practical needs of Japanese export shipbuilding. The Sumitomo investigation adds rare technical evidence about Japanese wartime radar development, including direct copying from captured or recovered B-29 equipment and attempted jamming trials. Duplicate directives and reports also preserve evidence of how enclosures circulated within the State Department, while the mismatch between the stated file dates and the actual contents illustrates later accretion within the decimal filing system.
